{{Short description|Graph invariant defined from axis-parallel unit cubes}}

[[File:A graph with cubicity 2.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|A graph with cubicity {{math|2}}, realized as the intersection graph of axis-parallel unit {{math|2}}-cubes, i.e. axis-parallel unit squares, in the plane.]]

In the mathematical field of [[graph theory]], '''cubicity''' is a [[graph invariant]] defined to be the smallest dimension such that a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] can be realized as the [[intersection graph]] of axis-parallel [[unit cube]]s in [[Euclidean space]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Fishburn|1983|page=309|loc=Section 1}}</ref> Cubicity was introduced by [[Fred S. Roberts]] in 1969, along with a related invariant called [[boxicity]] that considers the smallest dimension needed to represent a graph as the intersection graph of axis-parallel [[Hyperrectangle|rectangles]] in Euclidean space.<ref>{{harvtxt|Roberts|1969|pages=301–310}}</ref>

[[File:Indifference graph = unit interval graph.svg|thumb|310px|An [[indifference graph]] with cubicity {{math|1}}, realized as the intersection graph of unit {{math|1}}-cubes, i.e. unit intervals, on the real [[number line]].]]

== Definition ==
This article only considers [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|simple, undirected graphs]], with finite and non-empty vertex sets.<ref>{{harvtxt|Chandran|Mathew|2009|page=2|loc=Section 1}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Fishburn|1983|page=309|loc=Section 1}}</ref>

The ''cubicity'' of a graph <math>G</math>, denoted by <math>\operatorname{cub}(G)</math>, is the smallest [[integer]] <math>k</math> such that <math>G</math> can be represented as the intersection graph of axis-parallel [[Closed set|closed]] unit <math>k</math>-cubes in <math>k</math>-dimensional Euclidean space, <math>\mathrm{E}^k</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Roberts|1969|page=302|loc=Section 1}} uses closed cubes of side-length <math>1</math>.<br>Footnote 1 on p. 302: "Boxes are not necessarily closed, though it is not hard to show that if a representation [of <math>G</math>] is attainable with [open] boxes in <math>\mathrm{E}^k</math>, it is attainable with closed boxes in <math>\mathrm{E}^k</math>.".</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Chandran|Mathew|2009|page=2|loc=Section 1, Definition 4}} use [[Cartesian product]]s of closed intervals <math>[a_i, a_i + 1]</math>.</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Fishburn|1983|page=309|loc=Section 1}}</ref>

For <math>k \geq 1</math>, a graph <math>G</math> can have such a representation in <math>\mathrm{E}^k</math> [[if and only if]] <math>G</math> is the intersection of <math>k</math> indifference graphs on the same vertex set as <math>G</math>.{{sfnp|Roberts|1969|pages=302–303|loc=Section 2}}

The cubicity of a [[complete graph]] is defined to be zero.{{sfnp|Chandran|Mathew|2009|page=2|loc=Section 1, Definition 4}}

== Relations to certain graph classes, upper bound ==
For a graph <math>G</math>, <math>\operatorname{cub}(G) = 0</math> if and only if <math>G</math> is complete.{{sfnp|Roberts|1969|page=304|loc=Section 3, Proof of Theorem 2}}

For a graph <math>G</math>, <math>\operatorname{cub}(G) = 1</math> if and only if <math>G</math> is a [[unit interval graph]] that is not complete.{{sfnp|Fishburn|1983|page=310|loc=Section 1}}

For <math>n \in \N^*</math>, <math>\operatorname{cub}(K_{1,n}) = \lfloor \log_2 (2n-1) \rfloor</math>, where <math>K_{1,n}</math> denotes the [[star graph]], a tree with one internal vertex and <math>n</math> leaves, and where <math>\lfloor \cdot \rfloor</math> denotes the [[Floor and ceiling functions|floor function]].{{sfnp|Roberts|1969|page=303|loc=Section 3, Theorem 1}}

For <math>p \in \N^*</math>, <math>\operatorname{cub}(K_{p(2)}) = p</math>, where <math>K_{p(2)}</math> denotes the [[Multipartite graph|complete multipartite graph]] with <math>p</math> parts of [[Cardinal number|cardinal]] <math>2</math>.{{sfnp|Fishburn|1983|page=310|loc=Section 1}}{{sfnp|Roberts|1969|page=304|loc=Section 3, Theorem 2}}

For a graph <math>G</math> on <math>n</math> vertices, <math>\operatorname{cub}(G) \leq \lfloor 2n/3 \rfloor</math>. Moreover, this upper bound is best possible in terms of <math>n</math>.{{sfnp|Fishburn|1983|page=310|loc=Section 1}}{{sfnp|Roberts|1969|page=306|loc=Section 4, Theorem 5}}

== Relations to other graph dimensions ==
=== Relations to boxicity: bounds ===
The cubicity of a graph <math>G</math> is closely related to its boxicity, denoted by <math>\operatorname{box}(G).</math> The definition of boxicity is essentially the same as that of cubicity, but with axis-parallel [[Hyperrectangle|boxes]] instead of axis-parallel unit cubes.

Since a cube is a special case of a box, the cubicity of a graph <math>G</math> is always an upper bound for its boxicity, i.e., <math>~ \operatorname{box}(G) \leq \operatorname{cub}(G).</math>

In the other direction, it can be shown that for a graph <math>G</math> on <math>n</math> vertices, <math>~ \operatorname{cub}(G) \leq \lceil \log_2 n \rceil \operatorname{box}(G), ~</math> where <math>\lceil \cdot \rceil</math> denotes the [[Floor and ceiling functions|ceiling function]]. Moreover, this upper bound is tight.<ref>{{harvtxt|Chandran|Mathew|2009|page=3|loc=Section 2, Theorem 1}}</ref>

=== Relations to sphericity ===
The [[Sphericity (graph theory)|sphericity]] of a graph <math>G,</math> denoted by <math>\operatorname{sph}(G),</math> is defined in the same way as cubicity but with [[Congruence (geometry)|congruent]] [[sphere]]s instead of axis-parallel unit cubes.

For certain graphs, cubicity exceeds sphericity; the five-pointed star, <math>K_{1,5},</math> is an example: <math>~ \operatorname{cub}(K_{1,5}) = 3 > \operatorname{sph}(K_{1,5}) = 2.</math><ref>{{harvtxt|Fishburn|1983|page=309|loc=Section 1}}</ref>

In the other direction, graphs <math>G</math> can be constructed so that <math>~ \operatorname{sph}(G) > \operatorname{cub}(G) = k, ~</math> for <math>k \in \{ 2,3 \}.</math><ref>{{harvtxt|Fishburn|1983|pages=310–318|loc=Sections 2–3}}</ref>
